references.text: In [ref:Matt 23:25-26|Matthew 23:25-26], Jesus uses almost identical imagery regarding the Pharisees, who clean the outside of cups and dishes but inside are full of greed and self-indulgence. This is the parallel passage in Matthew.

In [ref:Matt 23:27-28|Matthew 23:27-28], Jesus expands the image with whitewashed tombs—beautiful on the outside, but inside full of dead men's bones and uncleanness. The same contrast between outward purity and inner impurity.
In [ref:Luk 11:40-41|Luke 11:40-41], Jesus continues his argument: he who made the outside also made the inside, and urges giving what is inside as alms, then everything will be clean.
In [ref:Mark 7:1-4|Mark 7:1-4], the Pharisees' practice of washing cups, pitchers, and copper vessels is described, illustrating their preoccupation with outward ritual purity that Jesus criticizes.

In [ref:Mark 7:20-23|Mark 7:20-23], Jesus teaches that it is what comes from within a person that makes them unclean—evil thoughts, greed, wickedness, etc. This reflects the terms ἁρπαγή (greed) and πονηρία (wickedness) in Luke 11:39.

In [ref:1 Sam 16:7|1 Samuel 16:7], the Lord says that people look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart. This is a fundamental Old Testament principle behind Jesus' criticism of the Pharisees' outward piety.

In [ref:Jes 29:13|Isaiah 29:13], the Lord complains that the people honor him with their lips, but their hearts are far away. The same contradiction between outward worship and inner attitude that Jesus addresses.
In [ref:Ordsp 4:23|Proverbs 4:23], it is urged: "Guard your heart above all else you guard, for life flows from it." The inner self is more important than the outer, which the Pharisees neglected.
In [ref:2 Tim 3:5|2 Timothy 3:5], there is a warning against those who have "a form of godliness but deny its power"—an attitude that reflects the Pharisees' outward purity without inner change.

In [ref:Tit 1:15-16|Titus 1:15-16], Paul writes that to the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure—their mind and conscience are corrupted. It contrasts inner impurity with outward confession.
